lessons.title: Order and linearity
lessons.summary: What makes an equation second order and linear, and why it needs two initial conditions.

pages.heading: The shape of a second-order linear equation

blocks.text: The order of a differential equation is the highest derivative of the unknown function that appears. A second-order equation for $y(t)$ involves $y''$ and possibly $y'$ and $y$, but nothing higher.

The equation is linear when $y$, $y'$ and $y''$ each appear only to the first power, are never multiplied together, and never sit inside another function such as $\sin y$ or $e^{y}$. Every second-order linear equation can be written as
The coefficients $a$, $b$, $c$ and the right-hand side $g$ may depend on $t$, but never on $y$. We always work on an interval where $a(t) \neq 0$.

pages.heading: Normalized form and a quick linearity check

blocks.text: Because $a(t)$ is nonzero on our interval, we may divide by it. This gives the normalized form used by the existence theorem and by variation of parameters:

items: $t^2 y'' + t y' - y = e^{t}$ is second order and linear (coefficients depend only on $t$).
$y'' + \sin y = 0$ (the full pendulum) is nonlinear, because $y$ sits inside a sine.
$y'' + y\,y' = 0$ is nonlinear, because it multiplies $y$ by $y'$.
$y''' + y = 0$ is linear but third order, so it is outside this guide.

blocks.text: The equation is homogeneous when $g(t) = 0$ for every $t$, and nonhomogeneous otherwise. Write $L[y] = a y'' + b y' + c y$ for the left-hand side. Differentiation is linear, so for any constants $C_1$ and $C_2$
So if $y_1$ and $y_2$ both solve $L[y] = 0$, every combination $C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2$ solves it too. This is the superposition principle.
When $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent (neither is a constant multiple of the other), $C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2$ is the general solution: every solution of the homogeneous equation has this form.

pages.heading: Two initial conditions pin down one solution

blocks.text: The general solution has two free constants, so we need two pieces of data. An initial value problem gives the value and the slope at one starting time $t_0$:
Existence and uniqueness: if $p$, $q$ and $f$ are continuous on an open interval containing $t_0$, then exactly one solution satisfies both conditions, and it exists on that whole interval.
For a moving mass this is natural: knowing where it starts and how fast it is moving determines all of its later motion. One condition alone leaves a whole family of possible curves.

lessons.title: Constant-coefficient homogeneous equations
lessons.summary: Guess an exponential, solve a quadratic, and read off one of three solution shapes.

blocks.text: Now let $a$, $b$, $c$ be constants with $a \neq 0$ and solve $a y'' + b y' + c y = 0$. Exponentials keep their shape when differentiated, so try $y = e^{rt}$. Then $y' = r e^{rt}$ and $y'' = r^2 e^{rt}$, and substituting gives
Since $e^{rt}$ is never zero, $y = e^{rt}$ is a solution exactly when $r$ solves the characteristic equation

blocks.caption: ManimGL animation: substituting $e^{rt}$ and factoring out the exponential.

blocks.text: If $\Delta > 0$ the roots $r_1 \neq r_2$ are real. Then $e^{r_1 t}$ and $e^{r_2 t}$ are two independent solutions, and
Example: $y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0$ has $r^2 - 3r + 2 = (r-1)(r-2)$, so $y = C_1 e^{t} + C_2 e^{2t}$. Graphs in this case cross zero at most once.
If $\Delta = 0$ there is only one root, $r = -b/(2a)$, so the guess gives only one exponential. The missing second solution is $t e^{rt}$. Substituting it into $L[y] = a y'' + b y' + c y$ gives

blocks.tex: L[t e^{rt}] = (a r^2 + b r + c)\, t e^{rt} + (2ar + b)\, e^{rt}

blocks.text: Both brackets vanish at a double root: the first because $r$ is a root, the second because $r = -b/(2a)$. So the general solution is
Writing $C_1 e^{rt} + C_2 e^{rt}$ is a common mistake. It is really one constant times $e^{rt}$ and cannot match two initial conditions.
If $\Delta < 0$ the roots are $r = \alpha \pm i\omega$ with $\alpha = -b/(2a)$ and $\omega = \sqrt{4ac - b^2}/(2|a|)$. Dividing by $|a|$ keeps $\omega > 0$ even when $a < 0$. Euler's formula gives

blocks.tex: e^{(\alpha + i\omega)t} = e^{\alpha t}(\cos \omega t + i \sin \omega t)

blocks.text: Because the coefficients are real, the real and imaginary parts are each real solutions. They are independent, so

blocks.tex: y = e^{\alpha t}\,(C_1 \cos \omega t + C_2 \sin \omega t)

blocks.text: The factor $e^{\alpha t}$ is an envelope, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the oscillation inside it.

pages.heading: The three cases side by side

items: $\Delta > 0$, real roots $r_1 \neq r_2$: $\; y = C_1 e^{r_1 t} + C_2 e^{r_2 t}$.
$\Delta = 0$, repeated root $r$: $\; y = (C_1 + C_2 t) e^{rt}$.
$\Delta < 0$, roots $\alpha \pm i\omega$: $\; y = e^{\alpha t}(C_1 \cos \omega t + C_2 \sin \omega t)$.

blocks.text: In every case, all solutions decay to zero exactly when every root has negative real part. A single solution (for example $y = 0$) can still decay when some other mode grows. Lesson 5 connects these cases to damping.

blocks.caption: ManimGL animation: where the roots sit in the complex plane and the curve each case produces.

lessons.title: Worked initial value problems
lessons.summary: Apply y(0) = y0 and y'(0) = v0 in each root case, one revealed step at a time.

pages.heading: A recipe for initial value problems

items: Write the characteristic equation $a r^2 + b r + c = 0$ and find its roots.
Write the general solution for that root case, with constants $C_1$ and $C_2$.
Differentiate the general solution.
Set $t = 0$ in $y$ and in $y'$ to get two linear equations for $C_1$ and $C_2$.
Solve, substitute back, and check $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$.

blocks.text: Apply initial conditions only after the general solution is complete. In nonhomogeneous problems that means after adding $y_p$.
The next three pages work one example from each root case. Reveal the steps one at a time and try to predict each step before you show it.

lessons.title: Nonhomogeneous equations
lessons.summary: y = yc + yp, undetermined coefficients, and what to do when the trial overlaps yc.

blocks.text: To solve $L[y] = g$, find one particular solution $y_p$ and the general solution $y_c$ of the homogeneous equation $L[y] = 0$. Then every solution is

blocks.tex: y = y_c + y_p = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2 + y_p

blocks.text: Why: if $Y$ is any solution, then $L[Y - y_p] = g - g = 0$, so $Y - y_p$ belongs to the homogeneous family.
Find $C_1$ and $C_2$ from the initial conditions using the full $y_c + y_p$, never $y_c$ alone.
For constant coefficients, and a forcing $g$ built from polynomials, exponentials, sines and cosines, guess a $y_p$ of the same family with unknown coefficients. Substitute it and match terms.

items: $g$ a polynomial of degree $n$: try $A_n t^n + \dots + A_1 t + A_0$.
$g = e^{kt}$: try $A e^{kt}$.
$g = \cos \omega t$ or $\sin \omega t$: try $A \cos \omega t + B \sin \omega t$, always with both terms.
$g = e^{kt}\cos \omega t$: try $e^{kt}(A \cos \omega t + B \sin \omega t)$.
A sum of such terms: treat each term separately and add the results (superposition).

pages.heading: Overlap: multiply the trial by t^s

blocks.text: If any term of the trial already solves the homogeneous equation, substituting it gives zero and no coefficient can be found. Fix this by multiplying the whole trial by $t^s$. Here $s \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ is the multiplicity of the matching characteristic root ($k$ for $e^{kt}$, or $k \pm i\omega$ for oscillating terms).

Example: $y'' - 2y' + y = e^{t}$. The characteristic root $r = 1$ is double, so $A e^{t}$ and $A t e^{t}$ both fail. The trial must be $A t^2 e^{t}$. Substituting gives $2A e^{t} = e^{t}$, so $y_p = \tfrac{1}{2} t^2 e^{t}$.

The undamped oscillator $y'' + y = 0$ has natural angular frequency $1$. Forcing it with $\sin t$, exactly at that frequency, makes the usual trial overlap with $y_c$. The particular solution then picks up a factor of $t$:

blocks.caption: ManimGL animation: the resonant response grows between the lines $\pm t/2$.

blocks.text: The method relies on derivatives of $g$ staying in a finite family. Forcings such as $\tan t$, $\sec t$, $1/t$ or $\ln t$ produce endless new terms, so no finite trial works. Variable coefficients break the method too.
For those cases use variation of parameters (Lesson 6), which works for any continuous forcing once two independent homogeneous solutions are known.

lessons.title: Springs, dampers and damping
lessons.summary: Read the root cases as underdamped, critically damped and overdamped motion.

blocks.text: A mass $m > 0$ on a spring of stiffness $k > 0$, with a damper of coefficient $b \ge 0$, feels a restoring force $-kx$ and a drag force $-bx'$. Newton's second law gives

blocks.tex: m x'' + b x' + k x = F(t)

blocks.text: With no external force ($F = 0$) this is the constant-coefficient homogeneous equation from Lesson 2, with $a = m$ and $c = k$. The explorer uses the letters $a$, $b$, $c$.
Since the roots have sum $-b/m$ and product $k/m > 0$, any $b > 0$ makes every root have negative real part. Damped motion therefore always dies out.
Compare $b^2$ with $4mk$, the discriminant test from Lesson 2:

items: Underdamped, $0 < b^2 < 4mk$: roots $\alpha \pm i\omega$ with $\alpha = -b/(2m)$. The mass oscillates inside a shrinking envelope $e^{\alpha t}$.

Critically damped, $b^2 = 4mk$: repeated root $-b/(2m)$. The motion is $(C_1 + C_2 t)e^{-bt/(2m)}$. This is the boundary between oscillating and creeping back. For a given mass and stiffness, a mass pulled aside and released from rest returns fastest without overshooting at critical damping.
Overdamped, $b^2 > 4mk$: two distinct negative roots. Released from rest, the mass creeps back more slowly than at critical damping.
With a nonzero starting velocity, critically damped and overdamped motion can cross equilibrium once, but never more than once.

blocks.text: With no damping the roots are purely imaginary, $\pm i\omega_0$ with $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$, and nothing decays:

The energy $\tfrac{1}{2} m (x')^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$ stays constant, so the amplitude $R$ never changes. Undamped motion is the limit of underdamping as $b \to 0$. It is the only case here that never settles, and it is the case where resonance (Lesson 4) can occur.
The explorer plots the exact solution of $a y'' + b y' + c y = 0$ for $0 \le t \le 8$, with $a > 0$, $c > 0$ and $b \ge 0$. Try these:

items: Start at Underdamped and slowly raise $b$ to $4$. The oscillation disappears exactly at critical damping.
Keep $v_0 = 0$ and raise $b$ further. Started from rest, overdamped curves return more slowly than the critical one.
Set $b = 0$. The envelope disappears, and changing $a$ or $c$ changes the period $2\pi\sqrt{a/c}$.
Set $y_0 = v_0 = 0$. The only solution is $y = 0$, as uniqueness says it must be.

lessons.title: Scope and next steps
lessons.summary: Why the shortcut needs constant coefficients, a Cauchy-Euler example, and variation of parameters.

blocks.text: Substituting $y = e^{rt}$ into an equation with variable coefficients gives $(a(t) r^2 + b(t) r + c(t))\, e^{rt} = 0$. A single constant $r$ would have to make the bracket vanish at every $t$, which generally cannot happen.

The characteristic polynomial, and with it the explorer, applies only to constant coefficients. Variable-coefficient equations need other ideas. One family with a clean answer is the Cauchy-Euler equation $a t^2 y'' + b t y' + c y = 0$ on $t > 0$, where the natural guess is a power $y = t^m$.
For the normalized equation $y'' + p(t) y' + q(t) y = f(t)$, suppose $y_1$ and $y_2$ are independent solutions of the homogeneous equation, with Wronskian
Then a particular solution is

blocks.tex: y_p = -y_1 \int \frac{y_2 f}{W}\, dt + y_2 \int \frac{y_1 f}{W}\, dt

blocks.text: Example: for $y'' + y = \sec t$ on $-\pi/2 < t < \pi/2$, take $y_1 = \cos t$ and $y_2 = \sin t$, so $W = 1$. This gives $y_p = \cos t \ln(\cos t) + t \sin t$.
This is a reference formula, not something the explorer does. Remember to normalize first, because $f$ here is $g/a$.

items: Laplace transforms handle discontinuous or impulsive forcing in constant-coefficient problems.
Rewriting $y'' + p y' + q y = f$ as a first-order system leads to phase planes and eigenvalues.
Power-series methods treat variable-coefficient equations such as Airy's equation $y'' - t y = 0$.
Numerical methods (Runge-Kutta) handle problems with no closed form.

blocks.text: The MIT OpenCourseWare materials under Further reading give more differential-equations background, and you can look up the topics above in any standard text. The explorer is a good place to build intuition for the constant-coefficient case first.

examples.title: Resonant forcing
examples.problem: Find a particular solution of $y'' + y = \sin t$.

steps.text: The usual trial $A\cos t + B\sin t$ lies in $y_c$, and $\pm i$ are simple roots. Multiply by $t$:
steps.tex: y_p = t\,u, \qquad u = A \cos t + B \sin t, \qquad u'' = -u

steps.text: The general solution is $C_1 \cos t + C_2 \sin t - \tfrac{t}{2}\cos t$. Its amplitude grows like $t/2$ without bound. This is resonance.
Try $y = t^m$, so $y' = m t^{m-1}$ and $y'' = m(m-1) t^{m-2}$. Every term becomes a multiple of $t^m$:
So $m = -1$ is a double root, which gives only $y_1 = t^{-1}$. For Cauchy-Euler the repeated case adds a factor of $\ln t$:

quiz.prompt: Which equation is second order and linear?
feedback: Correct. The coefficients $t^2$ and $e^{t}$ depend only on $t$, and $y$, $y'$, $y''$ appear to the first power.
Not linear: $y^2$ is the unknown raised to the second power.
Not linear: $y$ sits inside the sine function.
This one is linear, but $y'''$ makes it third order.

quiz.prompt: Why does a second-order initial value problem give both $y(t_0)$ and $y'(t_0)$?
choices: The general solution has two arbitrary constants, and two conditions fix them uniquely.
One condition is enough; the second is only a check.
Because the characteristic equation has two roots that must be equal.
feedback: Correct. Two independent conditions determine $C_1$ and $C_2$, and the existence and uniqueness theorem then gives exactly one solution.
No. Many solutions share the same $y(t_0)$ but have different slopes. The slope is extra information.
No. With one condition a whole one-parameter family of solutions remains.
No. The roots can be distinct, repeated or complex. The two conditions are unrelated to whether the roots are equal.

quiz.prompt: What is the general solution of $y'' + 4y' + 4y = 0$?
feedback: This is just $(C_1 + C_2)e^{-2t}$, one constant times one function. A repeated root needs the extra $t e^{rt}$ solution.
Correct. $r^2 + 4r + 4 = (r + 2)^2$ has the double root $-2$, so the basis is $e^{-2t}$ and $t e^{-2t}$.
Check the sign: $(r + 2)^2 = 0$ gives $r = -2$, not $+2$.
The discriminant is $16 - 16 = 0$, so the roots are real and repeated, not complex.

quiz.prompt: What are the characteristic roots of $y'' + 2y' + 5y = 0$?
feedback: The real part is $-b/(2a) = -2/2 = -1$, so it is negative.
This forgets to divide by $2a = 2$: $(-2 \pm \sqrt{-16})/2 = -1 \pm 2i$.
Correct. $r = (-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 20})/2 = -1 \pm 2i$, so $\alpha = -1$ and $\omega = 2$.
$(r + 1)(r + 5) = r^2 + 6r + 5$, not $r^2 + 2r + 5$. The discriminant is negative, so the roots are complex.

quiz.prompt: For $y = C_1 e^{t} + C_2 e^{2t}$ with $y(0) = 1$ and $y'(0) = 0$, what are the constants?
feedback: This satisfies $y(0) = 1$, but $y'(0) = C_1 + 2C_2 = 1 \neq 0$.
This has $y(0) = 1$, but $y'(0) = -1 + 4 = 3$. The roles are swapped.

quiz.prompt: Which trial particular solution should you use for $y'' - 3y' + 2y = e^{2t}$?
feedback: $e^{2t}$ already solves the homogeneous equation (roots $1$ and $2$), so this trial substitutes to zero.
Correct. $2$ is a simple root, so multiply by $t^1$. Substituting gives $A = 1$, so $y_p = t e^{2t}$.
Use $t^2$ only for a double root. Here $2$ is a simple root, so $t^1$ is enough.
$e^{t}$ solves the homogeneous equation and does not match the forcing $e^{2t}$.

quiz.prompt: Which is a particular solution of $y'' + y = \sin t$?
feedback: $\sin t$ solves $y'' + y = 0$, so any multiple of it gives $0$, not $\sin t$.
Correct. With $y_p = -\tfrac{t}{2}\cos t$ you get $y_p'' + y_p = \sin t$. The factor $t$ comes from the overlap with $y_c$.
Substituting gives $y_p'' + y_p = \cos t$, not $\sin t$. You need the cosine term.
A solution always exists for continuous forcing. It just needs the trial multiplied by $t$.

quiz.prompt: A mass $m = 1$ on a spring with $k = 4$. Which damping coefficient $b$ makes it critically damped?
feedback: With $b = 2$, $b^2 = 4 < 4mk = 16$, so the motion is underdamped.
Correct. Critical damping needs $b^2 = 4mk = 16$, so $b = 2\sqrt{mk} = 4$.
With $b = 8$, $b^2 = 64 > 16$, so the motion is overdamped.
$16$ is $4mk$, the critical value of $b^2$, not of $b$.
Undamped requires $b = 0$, but here $b = 5$.
Underdamped needs $b^2 < 4mk$, but $25 > 16$.
Critical needs $b^2 = 4mk$, but $25 \neq 16$.
Correct. $\Delta = 25 - 16 = 9 > 0$ gives the roots $-1$ and $-4$, both real and negative, so there is no oscillation.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about $t^2 y'' + 3t y' + y = 0$ on $t > 0$ is true?
choices: Substituting $y = e^{rt}$ gives the characteristic equation $r^2 + 3r + 1 = 0$.
Its general solution is $y = (C_1 + C_2 \ln t)/t$.
Its general solution is $y = (C_1 + C_2 t)\, e^{-t}$.
It cannot be solved because the coefficients are not constant.
feedback: The coefficients depend on $t$, so the exponential guess does not give a constant characteristic equation.
Correct. $y = t^m$ gives $(m + 1)^2 = 0$, a double exponent $m = -1$, so the basis is $t^{-1}$ and $t^{-1}\ln t$.
That solves $y'' + 2y' + y = 0$, a constant-coefficient equation. It does not solve this one.
Variable coefficients rule out the shortcut, not solvability. This Cauchy-Euler equation has a closed form.

quiz.prompt: In variation of parameters for $y'' + y = f(t)$ with $y_1 = \cos t$ and $y_2 = \sin t$, what is $W = y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2$?
feedback: $W = 0$ would mean the two solutions are dependent. Then the formula would divide by zero.
That is $\cos^2 t - \sin^2 t$. Check the sign of $y_1' = -\sin t$.
Watch the sign: $-y_1' y_2 = -(-\sin t)(\sin t) = +\sin^2 t$.
Correct. $W = \cos t \cdot \cos t - (-\sin t)\sin t = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$.

explorer.title: Live explorer: damped spring lab
explorer.scope: Constant-coefficient homogeneous mass-spring model $a y'' + b y' + c y = 0$ with $a > 0$, $c > 0$, $b \ge 0$. This is one subset of the course: it does not cover forcing or variable coefficients.
explorer.preset_policy: Presets set a, b and c only and keep your current y0 and v0. Reset restores all five sliders to their defaults.
explorer.zero_note: y0 = v0 = 0, so y(t) = 0 for every t. By uniqueness, the zero solution is the only one.
